Namibia has officially recognised its first three Other Effective Area‑based Conservation Measures (OECMs), showing that conservation goes beyond protected areas. OECMs are places managed to deliver long‑term biodiversity conservation, even though they are not formally declared protected areas, proving that people and nature can thrive together across working landscapes.  ✅ NamibRand Nature Reserve ✅ ProNamib Nature Reserve ✅ Canyon Nature Park  Together, these sites conserve around 318,480 hectares of land managed for biodiversity.  The certification followed a national validation workshop in Windhoek led by @ministry_of_environment_nam with partners including @namibia_nature_foundation , @mfmrnamibia, WWF Namibia, communal conservancies and others, supporting Namibia’s progress toward the 30 by 30 biodiversity target.  @namib_rand @pro.namib   #WWFNamibia #OECMs #InclusiveConservation #30by30

The Youth Climate Change Conference 2025 was successfully held from 4–5 November 2025 at the Emirates Hotel in Ondangwa, Oshana Region. The conference was convened under the theme: “Our Climate, Our Responsibility: Namibian Youth on Climate Action.” It brought together a wide and diverse representation, including government ministries, local authorities, academia, development partners, traditional leaders, media, youth leaders, learners, and children, totalling an estimated 157 participants. The event was spearheaded by SOS Children’s Villages Namibia through the Eco-Champions Project, with collaboration from partners and youth-led environmental organisations such as Youth4CAN, NAYORE, Tulonga Foundation, and Wakapinya Environmental Education.  The main objectives of the convening were to: Increase awareness among young people on climate change, its impacts, and their role in mitigation and adaptation, Build capacity through knowledge transfer on climate-smart practices, green entrepreneurship, climate finance, and resilience-building, Strengthen collaboration between youth and key stakeholders, including the Ministry of Environment, Forestry and Tourism, development agencies, academia, and local authorities, Provide a platform for youth-led dialogue, innovation, skills development, and policy advocacy and, Develop actionable commitments from youth and stakeholders towards climate resilience and sustainable development in Namibia. All these were achieved through presentations on various issues affecting youth and the environment, panel discussions, exhibitions to inspire youth to become innovators of ideas and break-out sessions tailored to create dialogues amongst youth on climate change mitigation.   Read more: https://youthforcan.org.na/2025/11/21/youth-climate-change-conference-namibia-2025/

World Hippo Day 🦛 
 Namibia’s rivers and wetlands are home to one of Africa’s most powerful and fascinating giants: the hippopotamus. Found in river systems like the Kunene, Kavango, Kwando and Zambezi, hippos play a vital role in maintaining healthy aquatic ecosystems. 
 As Namibia continues to champion community-based conservation, protecting hippos also means protecting livelihoods, biodiversity, and the delicate balance of our shared landscapes. 
 Let’s celebrate these incredible water giants and commit to safeguarding the wetlands and rivers they depend on.

World Pangolin Day | 21 February   Today, Namibia joins the world in celebrating one of nature’s most unique and most threatened species: the pangolin. These shy, scale-covered mammals play a vital role in controlling insect populations and maintaining healthy ecosystems.  In Namibia, pangolins face growing threats from illegal wildlife trade and habitat loss.   Protecting them means protecting our biodiversity and supporting the community-led conservation efforts that make our country a global leader in conservation.  Let’s stand together to protect Namibia’s pangolins because when we protect wildlife, we protect our future.🌎  #WorldPangolinDay #ProtectPangolins #NamibiaWildlife #CBNRM #ConservationNamibia

LEGAL HUB: Minister Indileni Daniel on Friday launched the Sustainable Wildlife Management Programme Legal Hub in Windhoek, describing it as a strategic step forward in strengthening Namibia’s policy and legal framework for sustainable management of natural resources.   The hub is a website containing a collection of policy and legal documents relating to the governance and regulation of natural resources in Namibia. Namibia joins other countries with similar hubs, such as Botswana, Zambia and Zimbabwe, to mention a few.   The online hub is a central repository of information pertaining wildlife management laws that can be a dependable resource for scholars, practitioners, journalists and broader public. It was done in collaboration with FAO Namibia.

Diceros bicornis. The black rhino’s name tells its story. Diceros comes from the Greek di and ceros, meaning two horns, while bicornis comes from the Latin bi and cornis, also meaning two horns. A name rooted in form, strength and ancient lineage.  In Namibia’s Kunene Region, these remarkable animals have adapted to one of the harshest environments on earth. Desert-adapted black rhinos endure extreme temperatures, survive days without water, and feed on hardy plants that few other mammals can tolerate. They move quietly through open spaces shaped by rock, wind and time.  Photo credit: @Marcus Westberg  #SaveTheRhinoTrust #BlackRhino

At Gobabeb, we are committed to developing the skills of young emerging environmental scientists. Vianda Kauzuu, an intern from @nustnamibia , presenting her research proposal on evaluating the effects of solar-distilled grey water on vegetables grown in distinct soil conditions. Her project aligns with Namibia’s Sixth National Development Plan (NDP6), particularly Pillar 3: Environmental Sustainability. In a country as water scarce as Namibia, her research explores innovative solutions by reusing grey water, reducing freshwater demand and using solar distillation, which supports climate-smart agriculture and renewable energy use. If you happen to visit Gobabeb and are interested in her work, feel free to chat with her, she’s always happy to share insights about her project and its importance for farmers facing water scarcity.

Here at Gobabeb, we value partnership and collaboration. Dr. Stephan Getzin, one of Gobabeb’s research associates, and his team mapped ring formation in the grass species Eragrostis nindensis across numerous study sites in Namibia from 2023-2025, representing the first in-depth investigation of plant ring patterns in the country. Gobabeb continues to provide a platform for both Namibian and international researchers to engage, innovate and contribute to long-term environmental research in the Namib Desert. Link to publication: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0140196326000601

BIOTRADE: Executive Director Sikongo Haihambo today revealed that Namibia’s biotrade sector contributes 4.5% to the national economy, with the country’s Devil’s Claw supplying 90% of the global market. Haihambo made the remarks at the opening of the Access and Benefit Sharing (ABS) Sector Training currently under way in Windhoek. He emphasised the critical role of researchers in implementing the ABS framework, describing them as the first point of contact with Namibia’s biological and genetic resources. He also acknowledged regulators as the guardians of the country’s genetic resources. Additionally, he highlighted the essential role of the media in raising awareness about biopiracy, benefit sharing and community rights relating to genetic and biological resources. The training, which begins today, aims to equip researchers, regulators and media practitioners with knowledge on ABS, and will conclude on 16 April 2026.

REVENUE: The Ministry generated N$183 million in entrance and conservation fees from national parks during the 2025-2026 financial year. A further N$109 million was raised from conservancies through joint ventures, concessions and conservation hunting.  Meanwhile, N$4.4 million has been invested in infrastructure development. Staff housing and office facilities at Hardap Game Park, Namutoni, Keetmanshoop and Daan Viljoen Game Park have been renovated. In addition, 183km of fencing in Etosha National Park has been upgraded, while a further 15km and 13km of fencing have been completed in Mahango National Park.  The upgrades are intended to strengthen tourism infrastructure, support conservation and wildlife management, reduce human-wildlife conflict, and promote biodiversity.

Over three days, key conservation stakeholders, including @ministry_of_environment_nam , conservancies, community forests, NGOs, researchers, and development partners, gathered in Windhoek to reflect on the past, assess the present, and shape the future of Namibia’s Community-Based Natural Resource Management #CBNRM programme.  The workshop unpacked several critical themes, including: 🔹 Governance and accountability within conservancies and community forests 🔹 Strengthening benefit-sharing and improving financial management systems 🔹 Enhancing tourism, concession, and joint-venture frameworks 🔹 Addressing human–wildlife conflict through community-led solutions 🔹 Modernising CBNRM data systems such as CONINFO, SMART, and digital monitoring tools 🔹 OECMs, landscape-level management, and transboundary conservation 🔹 Mining and land-use challenges in community conservation areas 🔹 Capacity building and accreditation through the NACSO Training Institute  These discussions were essential in charting a stronger, more accountable, and more resilient future for community conservation, ensuring that Namibia’s world-renowned CBNRM programme continues to deliver meaningful social, ecological, and economic benefits.

Earlier this month, our team set out to find a rhino that had not been seen for some time. With the help of a Piper Super Cub – an aircraft perfectly suited for low, slow and careful flying we took to the sky. Thanks to excellent air-to-ground communication using radios funded by the @namibia_nature_foundation Namibia Nature Foundation (NNF) , we located the animal just 30 minutes after take-off. Our ground team Jason and Epson once again proved why boots on the ground and skilled foot-tracking techniques remain irreplaceable in the work we do.   Now that we know this rhino is alive and well, we are focusing our patrol efforts on poaching hot-spot areas, especially after the heartbreaking loss of a cow and calf to poachers in October.  An eye in the sky played a key role in this successful search. Random aerial patrols not only help us locate rhinos faster, but also act as a deterrent to poachers and improve our reaction time. A huge thank you to Save the Rhino International for providing the funding to build this new capacity within SRT, and to all the supporters and funders who are contributing to our new air wing.   Special thanks to David Francis and his Super Cub for professional airmanship and some unforgettable views!  #savetherhinotrust #conservation #savetherhinointernational #namibianaturefoundation

Weekly Teacher Spotlight!  My name is Helena Frans. I was born and raised in Iishanaputa Uukolonkadhi, a small village in the Omusati region. I started my schooling at Iishanaputa Combined School from Grade 1 to 10, and completed my secondary education (Grade 11–12) at Mwaala High School.  Due to financial challenges, my parents could no longer afford for me to continue my studies. I stayed at home and began searching for work. In 2021, my uncle called me from the north to come stay with his daughter at Naankuse Lodge.   In 2023, a daycare was opened on the farm for all the babies, and I continued working as a house helper for my uncle. I didn’t give up.   A few months later, a vacancy for a school cleaner opened at Naankuse Primary School. I submitted my CV, and within a week, I was told I could start the following Monday. That’s where my journey truly began in 2023.   I didn’t stop at cleaning, I also helped in the daycare, assisted teachers with marking learners’ test papers, and supported learners with their homework. In October 2024, during a meeting with our boss, Mrs. Marlice van Vuuren, we were asked where we see ourselves in five years.  I shared my dream of becoming a teacher. My colleagues supported me because they had seen my passion and dedication, especially how I worked with learners and assisted in the Grade 1 class. As of June 2025, I was appointed as a Grade 0 & 1 Class Assistant.   In January 2026, I began my role as a pre-primary teacher. In February 2026, I joined Alison online learning and earned two certificates in Early Childhood Development.   I still dream of studying further and becoming a graduate. I believe my skills, dedication, and willingness to learn make me a strong future leader. I am proud of my journey and excited to keep growing with the Naankuse family.  Stories like Helena’s are made possible through support and opportunity. Wildlife Conservation Day - Okonjima | Namibia 🇳🇦   Wildlife Conservation Day on 4 December highlights global pressures on wildlife and the need for science-based conservation. At Okonjima and through the AfriCat Foundation, these priorities guide daily work. Long-term leopard and brown hyaena research provides essential data on population trends, movement and behaviour, supporting species protection in Namibia.   Monitoring also strengthens national efforts against illegal wildlife trade by identifying conflict drivers and vulnerability points. Okonjima’s 22,000-hectare reserve safeguards intact habitat and ecological connectivity, while its community-focused operations demonstrate how private landholders contribute to national conservation goals, from research and sustainable tourism to long-term habitat protection.  #africat #research #okonjima #wildlifeconservation #namibia   ____  © @pascal__ok | @riccoseebach

AfriCat Team Collars two more Brown Hyena 🎉  Two new brown hyena, a male and a female, have been successfully collared at Okonjima Nature Reserve, expanding AfriCat's long-term study on brown hyena ecology and social structure. The collaring was led by the AfriCat Research Team, with veterinary assistance from Dr. Gernot Redecker from the @windhoek_animal_hospital. Both individuals, estimated to be around three years old, were fitted with LoRa GPS collars designed to collect fine-scale spatial data while minimising disturbance to the animals.  Okonjima supports a naturally high density of brown hyena, as first described by Edwards et al. (2020) in "Socioecology of a high-density brown hyaena population within an enclosed reserve. "This density provides a unique opportunity to study how individuals share space and resources within an enclosed environment.  One of AfriCat's key research objectives is to better understand brown hyena social structure particularly the interactions that define a "clan" and how such groupings function within a high-density population.   While brown hyena are largely solitary foragers, they maintain loose social associations through overlapping home ranges, scent marking, and communal den use. The addition of these two collared individuals also allows AfriCat to examine whether their home ranges and foraging patterns overlap with those of previously studied hyena, contributing valuable comparative data to the long-term dataset.  Each new data point strengthens AfriCat's understanding of brown hyena ecology and advances our knowledge of this often-overlooked carnivore and its complex, nocturnal society.  #africat #research #brownhyena #hyena #conservation

Predator Above, Scavenger Below: The Balance of Hunger and Hierarchy   Within the Okonjima Nature Reserve, interactions between these two species are increasingly documented, providing valuable insight into how these carnivores coexist. During an evening game drive, Khaleesi, a collared adult female leopard, was observed feeding in an Acacia tortillas tree. While she fed, an unidentified brown hyena approached, pausing beneath the tree for approximately twenty minutes while maintaining visual focus on the feeding leopard. Khaleesi remained largely indifferent, continuing to feed as the hyena waited below. A typical predator–scavenger interaction pattern regularly noted within the reserve.   Such encounters reflect broader ecological processes known as intraguild dynamics between sympatric carnivores, which simply means how different meat-eating species sharing the same environment interact, compete, and adapt to one another. Research from Namibia, Botswana, and South Africa has shown that leopards and brown hyenas overlap spatially and temporally more than expected, suggesting complex behavioural strategies that allow coexistence. For leopards, hoisting prey into trees represents an adaptive behaviour to reduce kleptoparasitism. For brown hyenas, prolonged vigilance and scavenging opportunism allow efficient resource use without direct confrontation.   As AfriCat’s brown hyena research expands, a key objective is to document these interspecific interactions to better understand the balance between competition and coexistence. Continued monitoring will help assess whether brown hyena activity influences leopard prey access, cub survival, or resource distribution within the reserve. These questions are essential for understanding long-term ecosystem stability and carnivore population dynamics at Okonjima.   #africat #okonjima #research #leopard #conservation #wildlifeencounters

Two babies. Two critical moments. One urgent need. 👶🏽  At the Lifeline Clinic in Epukiro, volunteer doctors Dr. Annie Hollis and Dr. Chris Sefton are seeing first-hand how fragile life can be in the earliest moments.  One baby was born prematurely in the back of a truck during a 90-minute journey to hospital at 1am. His mother was critically ill. On arrival, he was rushed into care and placed on breathing support. Today, both mother and baby are in ICU and recovering.  Another, baby Christina, was born after an emergency call from a rural village 22km away. She arrived in poor condition, struggling to breathe. With limited equipment, a small team worked quickly to stabilise her using the only tools available. She is now recovering well.  These are not isolated cases.  They highlight a reality. Many delivery rooms are not equipped for even the most basic neonatal resuscitation. Sometimes, babies are born without something as simple as a towel to receive them.  Through the efforts of the Naankuse Foundation and the Lifeline Clinic, that is starting to change.  With the right equipment and training, more lives can be saved. Simple items like breathing support bags, masks, towels, and hats can mean the difference between life and loss.  You can help us change this. Support the Lifeline Clinic and help give every newborn a fighting chance: https://naankusefoundation.salsalabs.org/lifelineclinic/index.html #Naankuse #LifelineClinic

Data Collection Method: EPICOLLECT  Using the EpiCollect mobile app, researchers can record field data directly on their smartphones including GPS coordinates, photos, videos, and custom form entries, even in remote areas without internet access. This makes it ideal for field ecologists to collect metadata and field observations of their study site.   Once connected, data syncs automatically to a central, web-based project database, where it can be viewed, mapped, and downloaded in real time for analysis. This seamless integration between mobile and web allows multiple contributors, standardises data collection, and visualise results instantly across global study sites.   EpiCollect has transformed how researchers link smartphones to web applications, enabling faster, more reliable, and collaborative science in the field.  #africat #research #namibia #leopard #pangolin #wildlifeconservation #hyenas

Out in the field, a vehicle problem is never just a vehicle problem. A flat tyre, an overheating engine, or a missing tool kit can quickly become a safety issue and delay important conservation work. That is why our Ecology, Clinic, and Scat Dog teams recently took part in a two-part Vehicle Workshop at Cheetah Conservation Fund (CCF), hosted by mechanics Frans Kambanda and Esela Shipiki.  Staff from the Ecology, Clinic, and Scat Dog teams came together for practical, hands-on training in vehicle fluids, air filters, tool checks, tyre changing, and 4x4 driving. The aim was simple, to help build confidence, improve vehicle care, and ensure our teams can work as safely and effectively as possible in the field.  ‘It was really informative, everyone really appreciated the training,’ said CCF ecologist Utarera Katjavivi.   From checking fluids and air filters to changing tyres and practicing 4x4 driving, this training was all about building practical confidence for safe and effective fieldwork.  As ecology intern Saara Nghede highlighted, ‘I learned about the different parts of the vehicle and how they function, and also gained practical skills on how to change a flat tire. It was a very useful and hands-on session, and I really appreciate the opportunity to learn.’   CCF veterinarian Dr. Anne Shiimi added, ‘It was really helpful and eye-opening. I learned a lot, I didn’t know most of the things but now I can confidently say and tell how a car works beyond pressing pedals. And, I can confidently change a tire now.’   A big thank you to our mechanics for sharing these valuable skills. We hope to continue rolling out this type of training across other departments.    #fieldready  #conservation  #vehicleworkshop #fieldsafety #ccfcheetah

Update On Our Rhino Bull’s Eye 👀   We are delighted to share a progress update: the white rhino bull who underwent a delicate veterinary procedure to remove horn fragments from his eye last month is showing remarkable improvement!   His eye is far less swollen, the wound has largely closed, he’s even been seen socializing with a rhino companion he often frequents. The injury came after a fierce territorial showdown with another bull in which the sheer force of impact drove fragments of his rival’s horn into the tissue around his eye. These bulls were involved in two clashes, and the injured rhino was examined three times and only on the third examination were the fragments discovered by Dr Redecker from the Animal Hospital.   Dr Redecker has inferred that these fragments were likely lodged into the rhino’s face during the first clash and migrated to the eye area during the second fight. This resulted in the growth proud flesh, an excessive growth of healing tissue due to prolonged inflammation, around the eye, which was removed by the vet did full healing begin. 
  White rhinos have relatively limited visual acuity compared to their sense of smell and hearing, but healthy eye structure remains essential to protect against infection and maintain behaviour such as grazing safely. Though the extent of permanent vision loss remains under study, his prognosis is good we are still in awe of the power and resilience of these magnificent beasts especially considering he was walking around with the fragments of his rivals horn in his eye for nearly two months.  
 At AfriCat, we always prefer letting natural healing occur. But when an injury threatens survival, or when healing stalls under complications like proud flesh, intervention  becomes necessary. This recovery is a tribute to animal strength, veterinary skill, and the resilience of wildlife.  #africat #conservation #wildaid #namibia #whiterhino

Meet our Cheetah of the Month, Aidan! Aidan was rescued in Somaliland in August. He was one of ten cubs confiscated from wildlife traffickers, thanks to collaborative efforts of Somaliland’s Ministry of Environment and Climate Change (MoECC) and Cheetah Conservation Fund (CCF). At the time of his rescue, Aidan was estimated to be approximately seven months old. As one of the older cubs in the group, the young cubs looked to Aidan for comfort and reassurance.   After being rescued, Aidan and the other cubs were transferred to the Cheetah Rescue and Conservation Centre (CRCC) in Geed-Deeble. He was very dehydrated and malnourished when he arrived, and staff provided intensive care to prevent re-feeding syndrome and help Aidan build up his strength. After being tied up in captivity for months, Aidan also had difficulty walking. However, with specialized, round-the-clock care, Aidan was stabilized, gradually built up strength and began to thrive. In 2025, he was named by entrepreneur and philanthropist Simon Squibb (@simonsquibb), in honor of his son.   Today, Aidan lives in a large and naturalistic enclosure at the Cheetah Rescue and Conservation Centre (CRCC), where he is continuing his rehabilitation.   Want to sponsor Aidan - or one of the other cheetahs rescued from the illegal wildlife trade? 🐆 Visit cheetah.org/get-involved/ways-to-give/sponsor  #cheetah #wildlife #cats #wildliferehab #ccfcheetah

Approximately two weeks ago, Cheetah Conservation Fund (CCF) received information on two young cheetah cubs in the northeastern part of Somaliland destined for the illegal wildlife trade - if they survived. In partnership with the Ministry of Environment and Climate Change (MoECC), CCF quickly mobilized a rescue team to get the cubs as soon as possible.   By 7 pm the following evening, the cubs were safely back at the Cheetah Rescue and Conservation Centre (CRCC) in Geed-Deeble, receiving expert care. Thanks to the dedication and expertise of the team at the CRCC, the tiny cubs were stabilized and are growing fast!   The illegal wildlife trade continues to devastate wild cheetah populations in the Horn of Africa. According to estimates, fewer than 500 cheetahs remain in the wild in the Horn of Africa - and in 2023, the Northeast African cheetah, the subspecies found in the region, was uplisted to endangered. Most of the cheetah cubs removed from the wild as part of the illegal wildlife trade do not survive the traumatic conditions experienced while being trafficked.   🐆 Want to help stop the trade? Jabulani’s Journey   Since being collared, Jabulani’s movements have begun to tell the story of a young male coming into his own. Born at Okonjima in June 2022 to long-term resident female Lesedi, he spent his early life within his natal area. During his first year, he was frequently recorded within the home range of Sefu, who is considered his suspected father based on repeated associations during Jabulani’s early months.
  At around three years of age, Jabulani began to explore more widely. GPS data shows several months of ranging across the Reserve as he gradually moved away from his parents’ core areas. This exploratory phase is typical for a young male leopard searching for space and opportunity. More recently, Jabulani has settled in the southern reaches of Okonjima, far from where he was born.
  Encouragingly, he has been recorded with kills, suggesting he is hunting successfully and adapting well to his new range. And as the data is starting to hint… this young male may not be settling down 
 alone.   More on that soon.  #africat #leopard #research #wildlifeconservation #namibia   ___  © @pascal__ok

Last month, our ReGen lead farmers travelled to Kavango West for an agroforestry training with our partners from Aywa Forest Farm. All the way from northwest Namibia, traveling a thousand kilometers, they were amazed to see such a different part of their own country for the first time!   Last year, we slowly started introducing agroforestry in their gardens, and planted some first rows for them to get to know this innovative type of agriculture. These gardens, in De Riet, Fonteine and Ekoto, are amongst the first pilot gardens that ReGen Namibia will continue to build on, together with communities, our partners and tourism members. Capacity building by training lead farmers is an essential part of ReGen’s first phase.   For the lead farmers, this training at Aywa Forest Farm was about discovering what agroforestry has to offer. Agroforestry is still a relatively new concept worldwide and in Namibia, and so for them to see a mature system in practice was very inspiring. Experiencing a landscape where trees, crops and soil work together gave new perspective on how their own gardens can grow over time, and the benefits this provides for them.   Our farmers did not return empty-handed. Rabies claims the lives of more than 59,000 people worldwide every year - and nearly half of these deaths are children under the age of 15. More than 95% of rabies deaths are in Africa and Asia - and the majority of these fatalities result from dog bites. While this deadly zoonotic disease affects domestic animals, like dogs and cattle, the rabies virus can also be devastating for wildlife, especially endangered species. In shared landscapes, like Namibia’s communal farmlands, the disease can spread from domestic animals, to humans, and wildlife.   In Namibia, there is another connection between healthy dogs and cheetah survival. Many farming communities use Livestock Guarding Dogs (LGDs) to protect their livestock. With an intimidating presence and a naturally protective nature, these canine guardians deter wild predators, like cheetahs, and prevent conflicts between humans and wildlife. This means, keeping Livestock Guarding Dogs healthy also protects cheetahs and other predators.   Cheetah Conservation Fund (CCF) launched the rabies vaccination program in 2019 in the Greater Waterberg Landscape, building on the ‘One Health’ approach. Launching vaccination programs in remote regions comes with real challenges - but the program has continued to evolve. In 2022, CCF connected with the Global Alliance for Rabies Control (GARC) and in 2023 began using their digital tools. The difference has been significant, tracking data in real time - and making analysis much faster! We’ve also linked our data to the Namibian government’s reporting system, so our work contributes to the country’s national rabies prevention figures.   Last year, the program hit a big milestone 10,000 dogs and cats vaccinated. In Namibia, this ongoing and collaborative commitment to rabies outreach is building community trust - and saving the lives of humans, domestic animals and wildlife.   Want to learn more? Check out the CheetahTV episode with GARC’s (@rabiesalliance) Dr. Andre Coetzer, visit youtube.com/ccfcheetah  #conservation #rabies #wildlifeconservation #cheetahconservation #ccfcheetah

At the Convention on Migratory Species of Wild Animals (CMS COP15) in Brazil (March 23 -29), Zimbabwe has submitted a proposal to include cheetah populations in Botswana, Namibia and Zimbabwe on CMS Appendix I and II – the last cheetah populations not covered by the Convention’s highest level of protection. While the species was listed on Appendix I of CMS in 2009, cheetah populations in Zimbabwe were not included because the country was not a party at the time (but did join later, in 2012).   Zimbabwe was once home to the third largest cheetah population on earth. The cats were widespread in the country – and in 1999, the population was estimated to number more than 1,500 cheetahs. However, large-scale land use changes have caused Zimbabwe’s carnivore numbers to drop over the last two decades, including cheetahs. According to Zimbabwe’s most recent cheetah census (from 2022 to 2024), the country’s population has declined by nearly 90% since 2000.   Zimbabwe’s remaining cheetahs are at the core of southern Africa’s cheetah population – the largest wild cheetah population remaining on earth. Most of the cheetahs living in southern Africa are actually part of a single transboundary population stretching across southern Angola, Botswana, southwestern Mozambique, Namibia, northern South Africa, southern Zambia, and southwest Zimbabwe. These cats are also part of multiple transboundary conservation initiatives in the region, including the Kavango-Zambezi Transfrontier Conservation Area (or KAZA).  At CMS COP15, Zimbabwe’s proposal would add the last unlisted cheetah populations – in Botswana, Namibia and Zimbabwe – to the Convention’s highest level of protection. If adopted, the proposal would bring the entire species under full CMS protection. Cheetah Conservation Fund (CCF) strongly supports this proposal. This action is important – highlighting the need for an elevated level of protection for individual cheetah populations and emphasizing the importance of cross-border cooperation to save the species.   Want to learn more? Visit cheetah.org/events/ccf-at-cms-cop15-cross-border-protection-for-cheetahs/  #cheetah #conservation #CMSCOP15 #wildlife #ccfcheetah

Linking Leopard Lineages Across Time 🙌🏻  PP091, PP093 and PP137 are three young female leopard born at Okonjima Nature Reserve and recently collared as part of AfriCat’s multi-generational leopard study. PP091 descends from Isaskia, a female whose daughters continue to occupy space within the reserve, offering rare insight into long-term female site fidelity.  PP093 is a third-generation leopard and the granddaughter of Zani (PP034), a female first recorded at Okonjima in 2016 and central to the reserve’s early monitoring efforts. PP137 is a second-generation female and the daughter of Naya (PP018), a long-term resident recently treated following extended monitoring and minimal intervention.  Female leopard typically establish home ranges close to their natal areas, with dispersal decisions shaping population structure and density. By tracking related females simultaneously, researchers can examine how territories are inherited, how space is shared across generations, and how long-term protection supports population persistence. Together, these three leopard connect individual life histories into a single ecological record shaped by lineage, landscape, and time.  #africat #research #okonjima #leopard #conservation   ____  © @pascal__ok

Pangolin Proofing the Tech 👀  What you see here is one of the most carefully considered steps in pangolin research. In 2025, tag failure became a significant constraint on the AfriCat Pangolin Research Project. Pangolin move through burrows, dense vegetation and mud daily, placing constant mechanical stress on tracking devices. As a result, batteries depleted earlier than expected, antennas broke, and some tags detached from their attachment tabs and were lost underground.  The central challenge is attachment. Tags must remain in place long enough to generate meaningful movement data, but must also release if caught, to avoid injury. Achieving this balance is technically and ethically complex.  In response, AfriCat worked closely with @smartparks to refine both software and hardware. GPS fixes are now restricted to above ground activity to conserve battery life, and alternative antenna and attachment materials continue to be tested.  Progress in pangolin research depends on careful iteration, patience and prioritising animal welfare for this vulnerable species. We’re hoping the trials of 2025 have laid the groundwork for more reliable data in 2026.  #africat #research #conservation #pangolin #wildlifeconservation   ____  © @pascal__ok

33 Wildlife Immobilizations In 2025 🤯🙌🏻  AfriCat carried out 33 wildlife immobilisations, involving 21 #leopard, 9 #brownhyena and 3 white rhino. These carefully planned veterinary procedures support collaring for long-term research or medical treatment when necessary.   Immobilisations allow animals to be safely examined, treated, or fitted with tracking collars before being released back into the wild. The collars deployed during these events provide critical data on movement, behaviour, and space use, helping us understand how large mammals navigate a fenced reserve that remains ecologically connected to surrounding farmland.  While some followed standard protocols, others required rapid decisions and adaptation in the field. In every case, animal welfare remained the priority, and all animals recovered well and were released in good health and unharmed.  Some exciting highlights from this year include  • Removal of a horn fragment from the eye of a white rhino  • Surgical treatment of a lump on leopard Naya  • Brown hyena hot releases after collaring  • Leopards calmly exiting the wake-up crates  • Strong field teamwork during complex immobilisations  All procedures were carried out in close collaboration with our veterinary partners: Dr HO Reuter, Dr Anais Herbert,  Dr Gernot Redecker from the @windhoek_animal_hospital and Dr Ulf Tubbesing and Mariska Bijsterbosch from @wildlife_vets_namibia.   Some of these moments will be explored in more detail in upcoming posts.  #africat #research #wildlifeconservation   ____  © @pascal__ok

Imagine being small, vulnerable, and alone.  Two black-backed jackal pups — removed from conflict, orphaned, with no mother to guide them or protect them.   Now imagine those same two pups arriving at the Naankuse Foundation Wildlife Sanctuary… where they were given a second chance. Raised with unwavering care, yet always encouraged to remain wild. Two of our staff – Tresia Shihepo and Dr. Tim Hofmann –  presented at the African Wild Dogs United Conference 2026 (wilddogs.org), from March 10-12, 2026.   Tresia presented during the session ‘Pitches by Emerging African Wild Dog Scientists and Conservation Practitioners’ to obtain future funding for further genetics work. Despite strong competition, Tresia was awarded the grant! During the Genetics session, she also presented her Master’s thesis under the topic, ‘Assessing Relatedness of African Wild Dogs in Namibia’s Eastern Communal Conservancies.’   Tim presented during the Surveys & Monitoring session, sharing CCF’s wild dog paper ‘Using Scat Detection Dogs to Survey African Wild Dogs.’ One of the other talks mentioned CCF’s work specifically, as our research has demonstrated that scat detection dogs can find wild dog latrines and drastically increase monitoring efficiency. Tim also co-hosted a special session, ‘Exploring Wildlife Detection Dogs as a Novel Tool for African Wild Dog Research,’ with Jennifer Hartman from Rogue Detection Dogs.   A former veterinarian at CCF, Dr. Robin Gieling, presented a paper with several authors from CCF on African wild dog vaccinations done at CCF. All of the sessions were well attended and Tim and Tresia were excited  to represent CCF.   Scientific research is the backbone of our frontline conservation and education initiatives, and our scat detection team is vital. CCF’s trained scat detection dogs help geneticists find scat from cheetahs and other predators in the field. Once collected, DNA is extracted from the samples, allowing researchers to identify individual animals and better understand the population structure of cheetahs and other carnivores.   Just like cheetahs, endangered African wild dogs have disappeared from most of their historical range in Africa. Now Found primarily in southern Africa and the southern portion of East Africa, these  intelligent canids face many of the same threats as cheetahs, including habitat fragmentation, conflict with humans, and diseases transmitted by domestic animals. Next week, Cheetah Conservation Fund (CCF) is heading to the Convention on Migratory Species CoP15 (CMS COP15) in Brazil. So, why are cheetahs on the agenda at a summit on migratory species? Cheetahs are a wide-ranging and semi-nomadic species. In fact, the cats have typical home ranges of 800 to 1,500 square kilometers! For cheetahs, this is the wide-ranging behavior is a balance between the need to find prey, while also avoiding larger and stronger predators, which pose a potential threat.   Cheetahs also live at very low population densities. Just for perspective, on average there are rarely more than two cheetahs per 100 square kilometers in the wild. This means, for the species to survive, the cats need room to roam. In Africa, this wide-ranging behavior means the cats frequently cross jurisdictional boundaries between countries.   Today, Southern Africa is home to the largest cheetah population on the planet. More than half of the world’s remaining wild cheetahs live in a single transboundary population extending across multiple countries in the region. This means, cross-border cooperation is critical to save the species. As the only convention focusing exclusively on migratory species, the Convention on Migratory Species of Wild Animals (CMS) provides an important framework for protecting transboundary species, like cheetahs, establishing the groundwork for international coordination and cooperation.  Want to learn more? Visit cheetah.org  #cheetah #wildlifeconservation #conservation #cmscop15 #ccfcheetah

Nearly two-thirds of the planet’s big carnivores are threatened by extinction- including cheetahs. Over the last century, cheetahs have disappeared from most of their historical range, due to challenges like habitat loss, conflict with humans, and the illegal wildlife trade. Across the cheetah’s current range, climate change is exacerbating these challenges.   Returning cheetahs to the wild is a critical part of protecting the species. Rewilding can restore cheetah populations to their historic territory, and boost dwindling wild populations by enhancing genetic diversity. Cheetah Conservation Fund’s (CCF) approach to rewilding is rooted in science, supported by a research-based methodology involving rehabilitation, monitored releases, post-release tracking, and community-based protection systems. To ensure the cheetahs returned to the wild remain in the wild, CCF prioritizes supporting the communities living alongside the cats, launching initiatives like the predator Early Warning System (EWS) to alert farmers when cheetahs are on their land, and the Livestock Guarding Dog (LGD) program, offering a way to protect livestock without killing predators.   As predators, cheetahs have an outsized impact on the ecosystems they inhabit. Their presence helps to regulate prey populations and keeps disease outbreaks in check, and by dispersing herbivores and smaller carnivores, cheetahs also influence vegetation growth. The cascading impacts of these big carnivores boosts overall biodiversity, making ecosystems more productive and resilient. This ecological impact benefits humans too. Healthier ecosystems provide critical ecological services, generating benefits like improved soil and water quality.   Efforts to rewild large predators- like cheetahs - are already having an impact. Today, as we celebrate World Rewilding Day, we join a global movement to restore ecosystems and build a future where nature thrives.  Want to learn more? Last month saw the official launch of Africa’s first Wood Identification Screening Center (WISC) 🔬 at the Namibian Police Forensic Science Institute in Windhoek.   The event, hosted by the Namibia Police Force @namibianpoliceforce 🤝 in collaboration with the Ministry of Environment, Forestry and Tourism, @ministry_of_environment_nam  the Namibia Revenue Agency @namra_org_na , the United States Forest Service @u.s.forestservice , and the United States Embassy @usembnamibia , was officiated by Honourable Minister Lucia (Ministryofhome of Home Affairs, Immigration, Safety and Security), with remarks from Lieutenant General Joseph Shikongo (Inspector General, NAMPOL), Ambassador John Giordano (United States Ambassador to Namibia), Dr Beth Hahn (US Forest Service), and Commissioner Becker (Head of @namibianpoliceforce SI) 🇳🇦.   The center was established by the USDA Forest Service Office of International Programs and Trade, with funding from the U.S. Department of State’s Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs (INL), in close collaboration with the Government of Namibia and national enforcement authorities.   Why this matters⁉  Often overlooked, the illegal timber trade 🚫🪵 is among the most lucrative transnational crimes, undermining legitimate businesses, threatening sustainable livelihoods, and placing immense pressure on Namibia’s natural resources.   Globally, profits from illegal logging finance terrorist groups, drug cartels, and other criminal organisations. As one of the world’s largest timber traders, the United States has a strong interest in deterring illegal timber practices that undermine American industry, workers, and fuel large criminal enterprises.  By strengthening the ability to identify wood species 🔍 and verify timber shipments, the WISC will help prevent illegally sourced timber from entering both local and international markets.

Within just 14 days, he covered over 400 km, moving from our area of operation into Etosha, and has since wandered back out again, now recorded east of Outjo. Movements like his teach us a lot about how elephants use the landscape, how they respond to changing conditions, and how connectivity between areas matters more than ever, especially as climate and habitats shift. Understanding these patterns is key to adapting coexistence strategies for the future 🐘

POV: When Cloud insists on weighing herself.   Rescued as a young cub in 2018, Cloud in is now one of the oldest cheetahs at the Cheetah Rescue and Conservation Centre (CRCC) in Somaliland. She and her sister Mist were confiscated shortly after Somaliland began enforcing revised wildlife protection laws enacted in 2016. Her story is especially significant – not just because her rescue resulted in the conviction of two wildlife traffickers – but also because Cloud and her sister Mist both survived.   Ten years ago, when Cheetah Conservation Fund (CCF) first began working in Somaliland, there were no permanent facilities for rescued cheetahs and very limited veterinary training. In those early years before permanent facilities and trained care teams were in place, mortality among rescued cubs exceeded 50 percent. Over the last decade, that number has fallen to single digits – and in early 2025, no newly arrived cubs were lost.   Cloud has lived through the transition from the temporary Safe Houses in Hargeisa to the Cheetah Rescue and Conservation Centre (CRCC) in Geed-Deeble in 2023, where Cloud and her sister Mist now live in a large, natural enclosure. Cloud’s life reflects the arc of Somaliland’s progress in cheetah conservation – and the important improvements in infrastructure, training and veterinary readiness. Collecting data for a stronger future for giraffe in Zambia. 🇿🇲  Together with the Department of National Parks and Wildlife (DNPW), our team recently collected 🧬 DNA tissue samples from 51 giraffe 🦒 across 19 sites in Zambia, including protected areas, communal conservancies, and private game ranches and farms.  This important work forms part of the KAZA TFCA Giraffe Conservation Strategy (2022–2026) and aims to better understand the genetic diversity and population structure of Zambia’s giraffe for long-term conservation planning. 🌿  Using a non-invasive drop-dart technique, the team safely gathered samples and detailed data on age, sex, and location. The DNA will now undergo whole-genome analysis, with results expected in 2026 — helping guide conservation efforts across Zambia and beyond. 🌍  #GiraffeConservationFoundation #giraffeconservation #geneticstudies #giraffebiopsy #tissuesamples #genomeanalysis #GCF

🔬🦂 Understanding the small species that sustain our ecosystems... During recent fieldwork in Warmbad, the National Museum team collected arthropods and insects using pitfall traps as part of the @jrsbiodiversity project. These specimens are now being carefully sorted to order level, with further identification to species level by collection curators.  While often overlooked, these organisms play a critical role in maintaining ecosystem balance,  from nutrient cycling and soil health to supporting food webs. Studying them allows scientists to better understand biodiversity patterns, species distribution, and how ecosystems respond to environmental change.  This data is essential for informed conservation planning, helping to protect not only individual species, but the integrity and resilience of entire ecosystems.

Happy Valentine’s Day from our Livestock Guarding Dogs! For more than 30 years, these incredible dogs have been keeping cheetahs in the wild. Lately, most conversations around elephants in Namibia have been shaped by conflict. Crops destroyed, water points damaged, and in some cases, lives lost.  These are real and serious situations, and they deserve attention.  But at the same time, there is another side to this story that is often missed.  Across the country, people are learning how to live alongside elephants in a more informed and practical way. Not because it’s easy, but because it’s necessary.  One of the biggest shifts we see through EHRA’s PEACE Project is how quickly fear changes when understanding grows. Many participants arrive thinking elephants are unpredictable and dangerous. After the training, that perception often shifts.  As one participant shared: “I always thought elephants wanted to hurt you. But now I understand they don’t, if we don’t threaten them.”  Understanding behaviour, what attracts elephants, and what triggers them, can make a real difference in how situations are handled, especially in places where people are moving through elephant habitat every day.

Did you know? 🐘  Elephants communicate using deep infrasonic rumbles that can be as low as 12 Hz, far below the range of human hearing.  Other elephants can not only hear these rumbles up to 10 km away, but they can also be felt through the earth up to 25 km away, allowing herds to stay connected even when they are far apart.   📷: @conservation.diaries

In Namibia’s Eastern Communal Conservancies, vaccinating dogs and cats against rabies is one of the most important things we do to keep cheetahs safe. Rabies is a deadly virus that can spread between animals and humans. In shared landscapes, domestic animals – like dogs and cats – can transfer rabies to wildlife, and for endangered and threatened species like cheetahs and African wild dogs, a single rabies outbreak can be devastating.   There is also a connection between healthy dogs and cheetah survival. Many farming communities in Namibia rely on Livestock Guarding Dogs to protect their herds. These naturally protective canines prevent conflicts between humans and big carnivores by deterring wild predators – like cheetahs. Keeping these Livestock Guarding Dogs rabies free is essential to the whole system working.   Cheetah Conservation Fund’s (CCF) rabies vaccination program launched in 2019, in Namibia’s Greater Waterberg Landscape. By 2025, the program had vaccinated more than 10,000 domestic dogs and cats. Early on, the program relied on paper records, which were challenging to organize. In 2022, CCF connected with GARC- Rabies Alliance (@rabiesalliance) and in 2023 we began using their Data Platform, a free digital tool that helps organizations like CCF track and visualize vaccination data in real time. CCF’s work is directly supporting Namibia’s national rabies strategy – and the global ‘Zero by 30’, which aims to end human deaths from dog-transmitted rabies by 2030.   In Namibia, our ongoing commitment to rabies outreach and education is saving the lives of humans – and wildlife. For cheetah cubs, playing with their siblings and their mother is an important part of life. While the phenomenon is challenging for animal behavior scientists to study, most researchers agree play has an important developmental role for predators like cheetahs. By engaging in play with their siblings and mother, cheetah cubs are strengthening social bonds and cognitive ability, while also developing the skills they will need in the future, as wild predators.   Cheetah cubs have been observed engaging in four types of play: locomotor play, contact social play, and object play. Observed primarily in younger cubs, locomotor play - for instance chasing, jumping and climbing - is believed to help young cubs improve motor skills. Social and object play is often observed in older cubs, helping them to develop the skills needed to successfully stalk and take down their prey.   For young cheetahs, play helps the cats hone their hunting skills - and better prepares them for the challenging and unexpected situations they will face later in life, as adults.   #cheetah #cheetahcubs #cheetahconservation #fahlo #ccfcheetah

Life in the Namib doesn’t just survive, it specialises!!!!   New research by Treonis et al. (2026) explores nematodes living in hypersaline springs of the central Namib Desert.....and the results are striking. These extreme habitats host surprisingly distinct nematode communities, with some species showing clear specialisation to high-salt conditions. The study also found that salinity strongly shapes which species can survive, driving unique community composition even across nearby springs. Microbial mats were highlighted as key biological structures that further buffer extreme saline conditions.  For the full story: https://doi.org/10.1002/ece3.73328

Some of Gobabeb’s large 4700 Ah-2V batteries, to ensure 24/7 power, ruptured almost four months ago. The batteries were peak technology when installed in 2018 and were carefully maintained for extended use until 2030. Then they failed with a bang that was heard kilometers away. We could not replace the damaged cells or mix battery technologies, as it was obsolete technology. We required new LiPO4 batteries. Despite the looming festive season, SolSquare could assist Gobabeb to evaluate the cause of the damage, the suitability of our energy system for migration to modern technology, and now the installation of a new battery system. A long period of energy anxiety and power interruptions, with downstream damage to equipment, is eventually coming to an end. Thank you to Renette, Cassie, Leonhard, Jürgen, and the rest of the team for your help. #Solsquare

When drought dries up water sources, pressure rises for both people and elephants. They end up relying on the same scarce resources, and conflict becomes more likely.  For elders living remotely, like Ouma Elsie, this becomes a reality. Failed rains, damaged gardens, and elephants searching for food and water can quickly threaten a household’s stability.  Ouma Elsie has always adapted and persevered, like many rural residents do. But some challenges need extra support. EHRA assisted with a water tank, a solar pump, and garden protection to reduce risk and ease daily pressure.  Her garden was one of the first we ever attempted to protect. The wall helped, but it also taught us that some methods work better than others. Conservation often means testing, learning and improving as we go. Today, electric fencing has proven far more effective for garden protection.  Coexistence is not a fixed formula. It’s a process of listening, adjusting and working alongside communities who live with elephants every day 🐘  📽️: @conservation.diaries

In January, EHRA took part in a successful elephant collaring operation together with our partners.   Working alongside MEFT regional services, MEFT veterinarians Dr Janine Sharpe and Dr Lungowe Mary Sibalatani, helicopter pilot Carl-Heinz Moeller from AWCT, Johannes Kapner, our experienced EHRA ground teams, and local communities, several free roaming elephants were collared or re-collared to strengthen our Early Warning System and corridor work. These collars help us understand movements, anticipate where elephants may approach farms or villages, and respond proactively to reduce human-elephant conflict.  We’re happy to share that all collared and re-collared elephants have been closely monitored and are doing well. Tracking them has already taught us more about their movements, including one young bull who has since made his way all the way to Etosha.  Every collar adds to a bigger picture: better data, better planning, and safer coexistence for both people and elephants.  Thank you to every partner and team member who made this operation possible 🐘

Thirsty elephants can walk straight into a village, usually without warning.⁠ During dry seasons, most natural water sources dry up, and elephants get their water almost exclusively from boreholes.⁠ ⁠ GPS collars allow us to monitor movements in real time.⁠ When a collared elephant approaches a settlement, our early detection system alerts our team so we can warn communities in advance.⁠ ⁠ Early warning gives people time to prepare and avoid surprise encounters, keeping both people and elephants safer 🐘⁠ ⁠

Statement by Elephant-Human Relations Aid (EHRA):  Elephant-Human Relations Aid (EHRA) would like to address the recently published announcement regarding an elephant bull that damaged the roof of a house in Okongwe.  During the night, EHRA’s Elephant Guards responded immediately and successfully chased the bull away before the situation escalated further. Fortunately, no one was sleeping in the house at the time, and no injuries occurred.  The bull was attracted by Ana tree seed pods stored inside the house. Ana seed pods are a natural and highly preferred food source for elephants. They attract elephants much like sweets attract children. When seed pods or livestock feed are stored inside homes, this creates a known and significant risk of attracting elephants, especially during dry periods when their preferred food is scarce in riverbeds.  In situations like this, if there is no rapid response and preventative action, frustration and fear can quickly escalate, placing both people and elephants at risk.   The following day, EHRA arranged and funded the repair work, ensuring that members of the local community were employed to rebuild the damaged roof. We also convened an emergency meeting with residents to discuss the risks associated with storing seed pods inside living spaces and to explore safer storage solutions.  We strongly encourage residents not to store seed pods or livestock feed in structures where people sleep. If storage is necessary, it should be located away from sleeping areas and secured as safely as possible.  Desert-dwelling elephants are a protected and globally significant population, and their long-term survival depends on effective conflict mitigation rather than reactive measures.  EHRA will continue to share Early Warning Alerts with all residents. Our Elephant Guards remain on call to respond to conflict situations and to assist community members who feel unsafe or need help protecting their property.  For coexistence advice or emergency assistance, please contact a local EHRA Elephant Guard by the numbers given above.

Two spotted bush snakes were, quite literally, spotted at the pool at Ongava Lodge – a quiet moment that reminds us how seamlessly wildlife moves through this landscape.  The spotted bush snake (Philothamnus semivariegatus) is one of Namibia’s most common and widespread snake species. Slender, agile and usually a bright green marked with dark speckles, it is non-venomous and completely harmless to humans. These snakes are excellent climbers and are most often found in trees and shrubs, where they hunt geckos, frogs and small birds. On hot days, they may also be drawn to cooler, shaded areas – including pools.  Just another example of how, at Ongava, even a moment of stillness by the pool can turn into an unexpected encounter with Namibia’s remarkable biodiversity.

The Ocean in Focus Symposium in Swakopmund brought together over 70 participants united by one shared commitment, strengthening Namibia’s coastal and marine future.   Convened in partnership with the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, Water and Land Reform, the symposium created space for critical dialogue between science, policy and community voices all working toward a resilient blue economy.  From identifying marine knowledge gaps to unpacking coastal and marine-use impacts, key messages emerged: Climate change is already affecting marine biodiversity, including fish size and growth patterns demanding an integrated ecosystem-based approach. Underwater noise pollution remains an under-addressed threat, coupled with the ineffectiveness of sound EIAs to capture cumulative impacts. Strengthening the Small-Scale Fisheries model is essential to build resilience, sustainability and community-led stewardship. Across both days, one message stood clear, and that is science, policy and communities must move in step.  This initiative was made possible through a consortium of partners, with generous support from the Blue Action Fund and the Blue Benguela Partnership.

Hot off the Press!  How do you determine the age of a Welwitschia? It is commonly suggested that the largest Welwitschias in Namibia is about 2000 years old. But is it true? The only attempt to accurately date a Welwitschia was more than 60 years ago. In association with Sarah and Mike Martin at the Science Museum of the Norwegian University of Science and Technology, funded through a Peder Sather grant, we explored how to date a Welwitschia (see https://doi.org/10.1017/RDC.2025.10185). This relatively small Welwitschia was killed by horses in April 2021. It has been regularly monitored by Gobabeb since 1984 and was about 600 years old at depth, with a taproot of more than 6 m to reach water, and a cumulative leaf base width of 2.26 m. It implies the leaf bases were expanding at ca 3.76 mm per year (or 1.8 mm per leaf). If that is the case, how old would the largest Welwitschia be? The largest Welwitschia in Namibia is at the Messum, with a cumulative leaf base of 25m, and the largest on the Welwitschia Plains has a cumulative leaf base of 23.28 m. @vitenskapsmuseet_ntnu #vitenskapsmuseet #ntnuvitenskapsmuseet

What is #WorldFisheriesDay all about? This day is dedicated to highlighting the critical importance of sustainable fisheries, healthy aquatic ecosystems, and the livelihoods of fishing communities around the world.   The main aims and themes of the day include: 📌Promoting sustainable practices 📌Addressing threats and serious issues facing global fisheries, such as overfishing 📌Supporting small-scale fishers 📌Recognizing the vital role of fish as a crucial source of protein and food security for billions of people globally.  We champion sustainable inland fisheries through a holistic, community-led approach focused on the Kavango-Zambezi Transfrontier Conservation Area (KAZA). We work with  the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, Water and Land Reform (MAFWLR) to establish Community Co-managed Fish Reserves that have already shown promising signs of fish stock recovery. Tenebrionid beetles were central to the founding of Gobabeb and remain icons of desert adaptation. Many of these beetles are flightless. That may sound like a disadvantage, but it is actually a smart evolutionary trade-off for surviving extreme aridity. Their hard wing covers (elytra) are fused shut, creating a sealed subelytral cavity. Instead of breathing directly from dry desert air, beetles exchange gases inside this humid space, with air leaving through a restricted posterior opening. This design reduces water loss in hot, windy conditions. Even their black colour is not a problem. Although black absorbs heat, studies show that colour has only a small effect on body temperature. What matters more is behaviour. When it gets hot, beetles stilt, lifting their bodies off the sand to cool down in moving air. Photo credits: Huntley, B.J., 2023. Indigenous and Local Knowledge #ILK took its rightful place at the centre of Namibia’s biodiversity and conversation policies. For generations, Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities #IPLCs have safeguarded biodiversity through place-based knowledge systems, deeply rooted in daily interactions with nature. In Namibia, where 70% of the population depends on natural resources for food, medicine, fuel, and income, this knowledge is not optional, it’s essential. That’s why last month we hosted hosted a national workshop focused on integrating ILK into Namibia’s biodiversity strategies, including the upcoming NBSAP III. Discussions addressed the risks of knowledge erosion, the importance of co-created documentation, and the need for fair benefit-sharing mechanisms that respect intellectual property.  #ILK #IndigenousKnowledge #NamibiaConservation #Biodiversity #IPLCs #PolicyIntegration #UNESCO #MEFT #BenefitSharing #FutureOfConservation

Hot off the press! A recent article revealed relationships between the southernmost Welwitschia populations (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.celrep.2025.116836). It indicated that Welwitschia may have been more widespread during the Pliocene (ca 3 million years ago), but populations fragmented around the onset of Namib hyperaridity due to intensification of the Benguela upwelling system ca 2 million years ago. Around 500,000 years ago, the well-known Welwitschia Plains population at the Swakop River fragmented into a northern population around the big Welwitschia on the Husab plains, and the population near the Moon landscape south of the river, possibly due to a combination of factors that includes intensification of Swakop River flood events, a deeper river channel and greater aridity of the area. This research highlights why every Welwitschia population is special and why conservation of indigenous and endemic species should incorporate population genetic considerations. Very few countries can afford the type of cutting-edge technologies required for this kind of research, which emphasize the benefits of international collaboration. Masters student Adam started his measurements in the Kuiseb riverbed, surveying the area around Gobabeb to capture conditions ahead of flood events. Over the past three days, the work has focused on laser scanning, river channel surveys and sediment sampling, using a multi-band RTK GNSS receiver to ensure centimetre-level accuracy. The collected data will provide high-resolution insights into how flood events in the Kuiseb act as a barrier to the northward migration of the Namib Sand Sea. In addition, measurements from Gobabeb’s river gauge will be used to analyse the relationship between flood intensity and fluvial sediment flux. These datasets will also contribute to the calibration and assessment of a larger-scale model.

A fog cloud moved over Gobabeb the previous morning, reaching the crests of the dunes and lingering until about 07:30. Fog events here typically form in the early hours of the morning, often from around 02:00 onwards, and they remain one of the Namib Desert’s most important water sources in a landscape that may receive less than 20 mm of rain a year. Fog is carried inland by wind and can travel more than 100 km, sustaining organisms adapted to capture moisture from it. If you're visiting the station, early mornings offer the best chance to experience and photograph this remarkable desert phenomenon.

CONRAD (NAD) BRAIN 1963 - 2025  Today, Gobabeb staff and associates, past and present, honour one of our own, a remarkable Namibian soul – a wildlife vet, scientist, and pilot whose life was inextricably woven into the land he loved. Having been introduced to the Namib at an early age, Nad dedicated his days to the wild places of Namibia, more recently rekindling his association with Gobabeb.  Whether planning new projects to investigate longevity and health of the keystone fig trees in the Kuiseb, advising young postgraduate students on baboon behaviour, imagining the adventures of a very famous 4x4 hero, brainstorming ideas to ensure sustainability of the research facility, or lifting into the sky to track gemsbok from above, he lived with purpose, courage, and quiet generosity. But beyond these professional roles, he was simply a good man – kind, and impossibly humble. He gave without hesitation, without needing thanks. A subtle hint, and he had our students up the air on their first flying experience. A small gesture, perhaps, but leaving a huge and lasting affection for that tall, bare-footed, friendly figure in dusty overalls striding across the gravel plains en route to the airfield.  Today we celebrate a life lived boldly and compassionately. Though he has taken his final flight, his presence circles above us still — in the Namib Desert he loved, the wilderness he protected, and the lives he touched.

Since attending the initial Law Enforcement Training in September 2024, 22 nominated DoF personnel, used their real-world experiences presenting case studies, driving the discussions on gaps and challenges as well as the way forward.  The focus for the 1-week session included, illegal harvesting and trading of protected succulent plants, illegal logging of timber, and other forest produce. Did you know that around 20% of the world’s arid and hyper-arid regions are covered by aeolian dunes? Jabulani & Naleli 😻  Previously, we followed Jabulani’s transition from a northern-born cub to a southern resident male. Over the past year, he has consolidated his territory and grown increasingly confident within it. Naleli’s story unfolded alongside his. A young female establishing herself in the same southern region, she has secured her own space as she approaches reproductive maturity.  As both leopards strengthened their presence, their movements began to align. Over the past months, guides have recorded mating behaviour on four confirmed dates, and the pair are also seen regularly sharing kills, indicating repeated and deliberate association rather than chance encounters.  If successful, this union would connect long-standing northern and southern maternal lines within the Reserve. What began as separate dispersal and establishment stories may now represent the formation of a new breeding pair in Okonjima’s south.  #africat #research #leopard #namibia #conservation   ____ © @pascal__ok

So much about them is still unknown 🥺🥺🥺  Despite their ecological importance and growing conservation concern, Temminck’s pangolin remains one of the least understood mammals in southern Africa. Fundamental questions are still unresolved. How many pangolin live in a given area? How much space do they need? How far do young animals disperse? Which habitats do they rely on, and how do rainfall and drought affect their survival?  AfriCat’s Pangolin Research Project was established to address these gaps through long-term study of a wild, free-ranging population in Okonjima Nature Reserve. The project is explicitly interdisciplinary, combining population monitoring, movement ecology, foraging ecology, life-history tracking, and genetic analyses.   #africat #research #pangolin #wildlifeconservation #namibia   ____ © @pascal__ok

The Queen of Okonjima | Isaskia   This is, the leopard queen of Okonjima’s north-central region. Her name means “beautiful” in Khoekhoegowab, which is spoken by the Damara and Nama people of Namibia. A fitting description for this long-standing matriarch. Estimated to have been born in 2009, she is the oldest female in the Reserve at 17 years old. First observed as a young adult in 2011, later camera trap footage and DNA analysis revealed she is the daughter of past Okonjima resident Shira, a shy and seldom-seen female leopard from the north.  Isaskia has had three, possibly four, litters during her lifetime. Her last two daughters remain in the Reserve and are part of AfriCat’s ongoing research. Having been born in the Reserve, she is famously relaxed around vehicles, a trait she has passed on to her offspring. Tragically, all three of her sons have left the Reserve. While the fate of one remains unknown, one was illegally killed despite AfriCat’s efforts to protect him.  Her life illustrates the importance of monitoring young males, which is now being supported with LoRa GPS collars to track those who disperse. Isaskia’s story highlights both the resilience of female leopards and the challenges faced by males leaving the Reserve.  #africat #research #leopard #conservation #okonjima   ____  © @pascal__ok

What looks like a gentle rub against a branch is actually one of nature’s most precise communication tools.  Leopards maintain complex, overlapping territories. To manage these vast spaces without direct confrontation, they rely on a sophisticated multimodal scent-marking system.  Urine spraying, claw raking, and strategic scat placement all play a role. But facial gland secretion — deposited through deliberate cheek and forehead rubbing on vegetation and branches — is particularly fascinating. Each deposit carries a unique chemical signature, communicating individual identity, reproductive status, and recency of presence to any leopard that passes through.  #africat #namibia #wildlifeconservation #research #leopard   ___ © @pascal__ok

From Orphan to Mother | Amali   Amali’s journey at @okonjima_nature_reserve began with tragedy but has evolved into a story of strength. Born in 2016 to then long-term resident Jo Jo, she and her sister lost their mother at just 19 months in a rare event: Jo Jo was killed by a warthog, the only documented case of a non-leopard adult fatality in the Reserve.  Amali and her sister were left to fend for themselves, their survival closely monitored by AfriCat staff. Her sister disappeared in 2019, making Amali the last representative of her mother’s line in Okonjima. Now a mature female at ten years old, Amali has raised her first cub, Jambo, and has recently been seen with a new litter, continuing her mother’s legacy. Her story demonstrates the challenges of leopard survival, the importance of maternal lines, and the resilience needed to thrive in the wild. Time will reveal whether Jambo remains in the Reserve and how her current litter will fare.  #africat #research #okonjima #leopard #conservation   ____  © @pascal__ok

Hannah ended her internship with us by presenting the results of her project. To find out how soil properties, especially water-holding capacity, change within the hummocks of three different fog-harvesting plants in the Namib Desert.  The study aims to help understand spatial vegetation patterns in fog deserts and potential shifts in species dominance as a result of shifting fog patterns due to climate change. Acanthosicyos showed a statistically significant increase in water-holding capacity compared to bare sand. The changes were driven by structural properties, not chemical ones, with the coarse-grained fraction (<125µm) and Organic Matter as the main drivers.  Hannah also sampled along a fog gradient, choosing three sites at 20, 30 and 50km distance from the ocean. The results showed that there was no difference in the water-holding capacity, as decreasing salinity and increasing organic matter counteracted each other. This might suggest that fog oasis systems may be more resilient to spatial variability in fog input than expected. Overall, the results indicate strong interactions and co-dependence between the properties and show that plants follow different engineering strategies.

FIVE Brown Hyena added to our Research Project 🙌🏻  Over three nights in December, five brown hyenas stepped into the next phase of our research. Each was safely captured using our refined box trap system and fitted with a LoRa GPS collar. By coincidence, all five were female. OHB103 and OHB106 were familiar individuals whose original collars were nearing the end of their lifespan. Their recollaring maintains valuable longitudinal records. OHB106 was again visibly pregnant at capture. Her first collar enabled us to locate her den, and we continue to document activity at that site.  OHB103 appears to be reproductively active within a different clan network. The remaining three females represented new data points and new questions. Two were young animals, with minimal signs of wear. Subsequent movement patterns suggest OHB114 may be closely related to OHB106. OHB113, likely from another clan, lost her collar within weeks of deployment. The detached collar suggests intraspecific aggression, though her condition remains unknown.  The fifth female initially overlapped with the younger individuals before dispersing east beyond the Reserve. She has ranged between farms bordering the B1 highway and has recently shifted closer to her previous range.  Each collar now contributes to a clearer picture of female breeding  and clan dynamics, dispersal and landscape connectivity.   #africat #research #namibia #brownhyena #conservation   ____ © @pascal__ok

A Rare Look at Brown Hyena Motherhood  This is Malaki, one of the brown hyenas monitored by AfriCat researchers at Okonjima. Her name means “lucky” in Lozi, and recently she haslived up to it.  When Malaki (OHB106) was recollared in December, she was visibly pregnant. Later tracking data guided researchers and guides back to a den site, where camera footage has now confirmed the presence of two cubs.  Brown hyena cubs spend their first months hidden at the den while their mother returns regularly to nurse them, making sightings of early family life extremely rare.  Guests joining the Brown Hyena activity at Okonjima may be exploring the same landscape where Malaki is raising her young. With a bit of luck, a den site moment like this could become part of the experience.  #africat #research #brownhyena #okonjima #wildlifeconservation   ____ © @pascal__ok

Selene returns with a surprise 😍  Selene is a female pangolin first tagged in April 2021 as part of AfriCat’s early pangolin research. Over the following years, she was recorded giving birth and contributed rare insight into pangolin life history.  In late 2023, her GPS stopped working, and her VHF tag fell off. With no signal to follow, Selene was lost from the research. Equipment failure and the loss of monitored individuals are an unavoidable part of pangolin research and can create significant data gaps.  Nearly two years later, on 13 November 2025, Selene was re-identified after one of AfriCat’s pangolin trackers, Jacob, observed two pangolins emerging from a burrow, both without tags. One was a male whose tag had fallen off weeks earlier. The second was Selene, identified by her scale patterns. And she wasnt alone…she was accompanied by a pup on her back weighing 425g.  Her reappearance highlights the challenges of studying pangolins while reconnecting an interrupted research record and adding a new chapter to her story.  IMPORTANT NOTICE:  Pangolin welfare remains a high conservation priority. Recent data indicates escalating pangolin trafficking activity throughout Namibia, requiring enhanced surveillance protocols for our monitored population. We maintain regular visual confirmation of all tagged individuals to ensure their continued safety and wellbeing. This mother-offspring pair has been successfully observed during multiple subsequent field surveys, with both animals demonstrating positive health and behavioral indicators.  #africat #pangolin #research #wildlifeconservation #namibia
