Introducing NEO  The “One” of Okonjima. Named after the Matrix character, this nearly 12-year-old male entered the reserve as an adult, stepping into a new reality that would shape the next generation of leopard at Okonjima.  Over his decade-long residency, Neo has become a dominant presence in the heart of the reserve, holding the largest home range and earning his title as the “king in waiting” after Mawenzi. He has sired multiple cubs, including at least three with Vamos, and is often seen showing unusual tolerance towards his offspring, especially Mpandu. From feeding together to resting side by side, Neo challenges the idea of leopards as strictly solitary.  Now weighing 76 kg, Neo has taken over as the heaviest male in Okonjima, surpassing Mawenzi, who currently weighs around 70 kg, though still shy of Mawenzi’s peak of 80 kg. With strength, strategy, and surprising social flexibility, Neo is steadily shaping the future of Okonjima’s leopard lineage.  #africat #research #okonjima #leopard #conservation   ____ © @pascal__ok

Vamos 😍  You’ve likely already seen Vamos, she is Okonjima’s most observed leopard and at 8 years old, a true matriarch in the making. Her name means “let’s go” in Spanish, and it perfectly reflects her energy, determination, and dedication to her cubs.   Daughter of long-term resident Lila, Vamos inherited the northern portion of her mother’s territory, demonstrating a common mother-daughter sharing pattern in leopard. Guides frequently see her moving across her central home range, managing interactions with other adults like Neo, and protecting her young from threats, including opportunistic brown hyena.  Vamos has successfully raised at least one cub from each of her three litters - Yebo, Mpandu, and her current female cub, PP141 - balancing gentle parenting with fierce protection. Vamos demonstrates how female leopard balance maternal duties, territoriality, and social flexibility, ensuring the continuation of their lineage in a competitive environment.  #africat #research #conservation #leopard #okonjima   ___ © @pascal__ok | @nadiasnijders_photography

Many national parks occur in arid and hyper-arid regions, particularly within the Namib Desert. Though ecologically unique and supporting specialised biodiversity, they represent only a portion of Namibia’s biodiversity. More productive landscapes, including acacia savannas and thornbush shrublands, lie largely outside the formal protected area system. These environments support a high proportion of wildlife populations but are also the areas most intensively used for agriculture and livestock production.  Private nature reserves account for approximately 4% of Namibia’s land surface, forming a smaller but strategically important part of the national conservation mosaic. Happy International Hyena Day 🐺  Today, we celebrate one of Africa’s most misunderstood and often vilified carnivores, the brown hyena. Long entangled in folklore and misconception, it is far more than the stories suggest. This is a highly adapted scavenger-predator, quietly shaping nutrient flows, recycling biomass, and linking predator communities across Namibia’s landscapes in ways that often go unseen.  At Okonjima Nature Reserve, long-term research is steadily reshaping how this species is understood. What emerges is a picture of complexity: structured clans moving across shared landscapes, individuals ranging over vast distances at night, and close ecological interactions with other large carnivores, particularly leopard, where feeding opportunities briefly concentrate life across the system.  Through GPS tracking, camera trapping, and sustained field observation, Africat is revealing a species that is rarely encountered yet constantly active within the ecosystem.  Stay tuned for an update on our Brown Hyena Project later this week…  #africat #research #wildlifeconservation #hyena #okonjima  ___© @pascal__ok

FOREST RESERVES: The Ministry, through the NILALEG Project, on Wednesday launched the Hamweyi, Kanovlei and Zambezi State Forest Reserves in Windhoek. The launch follows the promulgation of these reserves in the Kavango West, Otjozondjupa and Zambezi regions in 2022, in line with the Forest Act of 2001. The reserves seek to promote sustainable access by communities to forestry products such as wood for energy and grazing for communal farmers, among others.  In a speech read on her behalf by Executive Director Sikongo Haihambo, Minister Indileni Daniel said the reserves represent the Government’s move to secure ecologically important landscapes under formal protection, in line with Article 95 (l) of the Constitution, which mandates the State to safeguard ecosystems and biodiversity and ensure the sustainable use of natural resources for present and future generations.  The event was attended by Zambezi Governor Dorothy Kabula, Kavango West Governor Verna Sinimbo, Khomas Governor Sam Nujoma Junior, and Tsumkwe Constituency Councillor Petrus Mutji, representing Otjozondjupa Governor John //Khamuseb, as well as UNDP Namibia Deputy Resident Representative Dr Christian Shingiro. Representatives of traditional leaders, Environmental Commissioner Timoteus Mufeti, and Forestry Director Johnson Ndokosho were also in attendance.

We have exciting news to share! Our cheetah keeper, Elifas Nashini, contributed a poster and an online presentation to the 6th International Meeting on Zoo Research, Conservation and Biodiversity, hosted by our longtime supporter, the Serengeti Park (@serengetiparkhodenhagen) in Hodenhagen, Germany.   Titled ‘Reducing Stress in Captive Cheetahs via Positive Reinforcement Training’, the poster submitted by Elifas outlines the way the cheetah team at Cheetah Conservation Fund (CCF) trains our cats to voluntarily participate in medical procedures such as blood draws through Positive Reinforcement Training (PRT). This approach significantly reduces stress during these procedures and ultimately improves the welfare of our resident cheetahs, while enhancing keeper safety.   The poster was designed by Elifas, with support from head cheetah keeper Lea Petersen, conservation scientist and canines specialist Dr. Tim Hofmann, and Dr. Laurie Marker, founder and executive director of CCF. This team also contributed to the development of the training approach, which is carried out by the cheetah keepers. Currently, all of the cheetahs at the Cheetah Rescue and Conservation Centre (CRCC) in Somaliland and three-fourths of the cheetahs at CCF’s Centre in Namibia have been trained with this approach.  Want to learn more? Visit cheetah.org  #cheetah #cheetahconservation #wildlifeconservation #bigcats #ccfcheetah

BIOMASS: The Ministry will spend N$155.4 million to support the conversion of bush biomass into value-added products such as charcoal, woodchips, firewood and biochar during the 2026-2027 financial year. The initiative aims to curb bush encroachment while promoting sustainable rangeland management, supported by a national forestry inventory.  To strengthen community participation in forestry, the Ministry plans to gazette three community forests covering approximately 360,000 hectares. It will also review the Forest Act and its regulations to address emerging and contemporary challenges.  In addition, the Ministry is developing a national wildfire management policy to strengthen fire prevention and control measures at national level.

Adaptive Research Methods for Brown Hyena  Capturing brown hyena for collaring is one of the more challenging aspects of carnivore research. Free darting of uncollared individuals is avoided entirely, as losing visual contact with a darted animal can be fatal. For this reason, AfriCat continually refines its immobilisation methods to prioritise safety.  Past experiences showed that brown hyena panic in standard box traps, while oral sedation carried unacceptable risks for both target and non-target species. In response, a new trapping method was trialled this year. Box traps were introduced gradually, padded to prevent injury, and monitored using cameras already installed at nearby leopard traps.  This setup allowed us to observe hyena entering the trap calmly and ensured an immediate response once the trap was triggered. Over three nights, five brown hyena were successfully immobilised with no injuries and minimal stress. Future upgrades will mirror leopard systems, including beam-trigger alerts linked to mobile phones and manual trap closure, allowing greater selectivity.  In upcoming posts, we will profile the five female brown hyena successfully collared using this method and share what their data are already revealing.  #africat #research #hyena #conservation #namibia   _____  © @pascal__ok

Most Trafficked Mammal on Earth 🌍   Today is #worldpangolinday, a day dedicated to one of the most extraordinary and most threatened mammals on Earth.  Pangolins are the most trafficked mammals globally. Across Africa and Asia, they face relentless pressure from illegal trade, habitat loss, fencing, and expanding infrastructure. Their decline is largely silent because they are nocturnal, solitary, and rarely seen. Yet their ecological role is immense. A single pangolin can consume millions of ants and termites each year, helping regulate insect populations and maintain soil health. Their digging improves aeration and nutrient cycling, supporting broader ecosystem function.  AfriCat’s commitment to pangolin research began in 2017 with a focused pilot study, laying the groundwork for what would become a comprehensive long-term research programme. Over the years, this sustained effort has expanded in scope and depth, enabling the systematic study of population ecology, movement, genetics, and habitat use within a free-ranging population at Okonjima.  World Pangolin Day is a reminder that awareness must translate into action. Protecting pangolins requires research, policy enforcement, habitat protection, and collective responsibility.  Today, we stand with pangolins worldwide.  #africat #okonjima #conservation #pangolinconservation   ____  © @pascal__ok

Himeezembi – our lion hero.  From the brink of near lethal human–wildlife conflict to the power and pride of a prime predator, Himeezembi’s journey is nothing short of extraordinary. Once emaciated and fighting for survival, this magnificent male was rehabilitated at the Shiloh Wildlife Sanctuary, where he reclaimed his strength, his spirit, and his roar.  His next chapter led him to freedom — translocated by Naankuse to the vast conservation landscapes of the TimBila Nature Reserve. Spanning 35,000 hectares, TimBila is now home to several rehabilitated, desert-adapted lions, each with their own story of survival after extreme conflict.  But life in the wild is never without challenges. After a tough encounter with two dominant lions, Himeezembi came off second best. His injuries required intensive care and time in a rehabilitation boma — a pause in his journey, but not the end of it.  Today, we’re thrilled to share the news we’ve all been waiting for: Himeezembi has healed beautifully and has been released back onto the reserve, now in an area where rival males won’t stand in his way.  Strong. Resilient. Free once more. Go well, Himeezembi. 🧡🦁  www.naankuse.com #naankuse #naankusefoundation #lions #bigcats #conservation #humanwildlifeconflict #animalrehabilitation

This week, a project from visiting scientists led by Manuel Herzog from the University of Heidelberg took us deep into the dunes to study star dunes, also known as mega-dunes. These impressive formations develop under complex wind regimes, where strong winds from multiple directions shape and reshape the dunes over time. The team collected sand samples from the top and carried out detailed laser measurements to monitor crest movement and surface changes. An additional sampling site includes Sossusvlei, with plans for repeated visits over the coming years to build a long-term dataset. We look forward to continuing collaboration and to the new insights this research will bring into dune dynamics.

WOOD SCREENING: The Ministry’s Forestry Director Johnson Ndokosho says Namibia is set to improve its control measures to manage timber trafficking with Africa’s first Wood Identification and Screening Centre. He said this on the margins of the Centre’s official launch in Windhoek on Friday.   The centre was launched by Home Affairs, Immigration, Safety and Security Minister Lucia Iipumbu and will be utilised by law enforcements to help identify and reduce the illegal trafficking of timber.   This centre places Namibia in a better position to manage and preserve its forestry resources as it helps to detect different types of timber, including those that are protected and illegal to transported without a permit. The centre was donated by the USDA Forest Service Office of International Programmes and Trade.

Did you know that brown hyenas eat !Nara melons?  During our monthly !Nara monitoring, we came across brown hyena tracks and scat containing !Nara seeds. While it is commonly known that black-backed jackals (Lupulella mesomelas) feed on the !Nara melons and play an important role in seed dispersal, it was fascinating to observe that the brown hyena (Hyaena brunnea), typically regarded as a carnivore, has adapted to the harsh conditions and limited food availability of the Namib Desert by supplementing its diet with !Nara melons. In doing so, it too contributes to the dispersal of this remarkable desert plant.

Did you know that fly identification relies on extremely small structures that most people overlook? Taxonomists depend on details such as bristle placement, vein intersections, tiny leg spurs, and even the orientation of individual setae. If these features are blocked by a folded wing or a badly placed pin, the specimen becomes far less useful for identification. Well-pinned specimens should not obscure diagnostic features. Wings should be fully spread, legs positioned so all segments are visible, and the antennae, mouthparts, and thoracic sutures unobstructed. No spur or scutellar feature should disappear under glue, foam, or poor handling. Dipterists are few worldwide, and likely none currently in Namibia, so if you want your fly identified, your chances are far better when the specimen is properly pinned.

BRIEFING: Environmental Commissioner Timoteus Mufeti and Atomic Energy and Radiation Protection Authority Director Axel Tibinyane on Wednesday briefed the media on the in-situ leach (ISL) uranium mining independent technical review team’s recent visit to Namibia.   The review follows Headspring Invetments’ intention to advance the project from prospecting activities to drilling testing wells using the ISL method. The independent technical review mission comes from the International Atomic Energy Agency to assess the proposed project in the Leonardville area of the Omaheke Region.  Mufeti said no mining licence has been granted to Headspring yet. The company currently holds an exploration licence, and to date, approximately 65% to 70% of the exploration work has been completed,” he said.   Considering the potential environmental impact, the government has sought third-party expertise and technical knowledge, as provided for under the Environmental Management Act. The review team will submit a report to the government and the government shall inform the public of its decision in due course.

In a hyper-arid environment where annual precipitation is extremely low and highly variable, such episodic rainfall provides an important moisture pulse. Even small events like this can trigger rapid vegetation responses and stimulate microbial activity across the desert. Here, every millimetre counts in shaping ecosystem dynamics.

Out of Her Mother’s Shadow | Naleli   Meet Naleli, a young leopard in the emerging cohort of female leopards, navigating the pivotal transition from maternal dependence to establishing her own territory.  Born in late 2022 to Lila, the dominant female of the Reserve’s south, Naleli first appeared in our records in April 2023 alongside a sibling that was sadly lost later that year. Initially cautious and seldom seen, she gradually became more tolerant of human observation, likely influenced by her mother’s regular presence. As her dispersal began, she revealed an unexpected aptitude for exploiting small structural gaps, repeatedly entering and exiting fenced sections of the Reserve. even pulling her first small prey items through the same spaces.  Today, Naleli occupies the southern portion of Lila’s home range, while her sister Vamos has settled to the north. This spatial arrangement allows their mother to maintain proximity to both daughters.   As Naleli consolidates her territory and gains independence, she stands at the threshold of reproductive maturity, representing the next generation of leopards that will continue the legacy of Okonjima’s iconic big cats.  Early observations suggest Naleli has begun interacting with Jabulani, who has recently also settled in the southern reaches of the Reserve, hinting at the beginnings of a new pairing in Okonjima’s leopard population.  #africat #research #leopard #okonjima #wildlifeconservation   ____  © @pascal__ok

SUBMISSION: Minister Indileni Daniel received a submission from Fumu Erwin Mbambo of the Hambukushu Traditional Authority on Saturday in the Mukwe Constituency of Kavango East Region. The submission contains a dossier of documents detailing concerns of the traditional authority on a variety of issues, including the Bwabwata National Park management.  Minister Daniel said she will consult and respond to the submission in due course.   Executive Director Sikongo Haihambo, Natural Resources Management Deputy Executive Director Colgar Sikopo and other senior ministerial officials accompanied the Minister. Kavango East Regional Governor Hamunyera Hambyuka and Mukwe Constituency Councillor Augusta Katembo as well as Regional Police Commander Commissioner Andreas Haingura were also present.

REFLECTION: Minister Indileni Daniel on Friday reflected on the Ministry’s 2025 work during a staff meeting in Windhoek. Highlighting the Ministry’s successes and shortcomings, the Minister commended the dedication of staff in the regions across various programmes for their continued service delivery under difficult conditions.  “Rangers and wardens safeguarded protected areas and wildlife, forestry officials worked with communities to promote sustainable resource use, tourism officers supported recovery initiatives…,” she said.  She added that resource constraints and increasing workloads were among the Ministry’s challenges during 2025.  During this financial year, the Ministry received a N$70 million development budget across nine programmes and 38 capital projects. So far, 45% of the budget has been utilised, with key projects completed, including the Fish River Canyon water pipeline, the Okahandja Forestry Office, road upgrades in Etosha and infrastructure at Ngoma, Namutoni and other sites.  The Minister also set the tone for 2026, calling for improved internal communication and proactiveness. The meeting was attended by head office staff, with regional staff joining virtually.

Meet Geraldine Gases, a resilient woman from Anigab who now lives in Irene Pos.  For years, she struggled to keep her garden alive as elephants repeatedly destroyed her crops. In 2023, EHRA installed an electric fence around her fruit and vegetable garden, and since then, Geraldine has been planting every summer. Now she looks forward to elephants visiting her homestead, especially when her grandchildren are around to see them 🩶  Through our PEACE Project, she’s also learned practical ways to coexist with elephants, gaining a deeper understanding of their behaviour and how to protect her livelihood safely.  We’ll soon be sharing more of Geraldine’s story and the valuable tips she’s learned about living alongside elephants. Stay tuned 🐘  📷: @laura_braune

What an exciting week…  The NBSAP III National Validation Workshop was held in Windhoek earlier this week. Sessions covered the NBSAP III process, and the review of action plans under Goals 1 to 3 through group discussions and plenary feedback, with good progress and great engagement from all stakeholders.   The workshop served as a critical platform to present the draft NBSAP III for review and validation and brought together stakeholders from across sectors to assess the proposed national biodiversity priorities and targets, confirm the integration of regional and sectoral perspectives, and identify any outstanding issues related to implementation and coordination.   The workshop also underscored the importance of inclusive participation, particularly in ensuring that regional perspectives and stakeholder inputs are meaningfully reflected in the final strategy.  Our work is never done alone. A huge thank you to all our partners and stakeholders who came together, shared their expertise, and helped bring this to life. Your collaboration, commitment, and trust continue to drive meaningful impact where it matters most.

CLEAN-UP: Opuwo - As the Festive Season Environmental Awareness Campaign continues to roll out across the country, Opuwo Town was the latest stop in promoting cleaner and healthier communities. Officials from the Ministry of Environment, Forestry and Tourism, the Ministry of Information and Communication Technology, and Environmental Investment Fund engaged motorists and residents on responsible waste disposal practices.  Plastic bags were distributed to motorists to discourage littering from vehicles and to encourage proper waste management along the roads leading into and around Opuwo. At the same time, outreach activities took place within the town, where officials interacted with community members, shared key environmental messages, and took part in clean-up activities in selected areas.  The campaign continues to call on all residents and travellers to play their part in keeping towns, roads, and public spaces clean this festive season, reinforcing the shared responsibility of protecting the environment for present and future generations.

What an inspiring day at the Annual General Meeting of the Namibian Chamber of Environment yesterday, whereby more than half of their members were present. All sharing one common goal, to conserve Namibia’s natural heritage and uplift its people in the many ways we can. We got an update of all the important work NCE has been doing, advocating for the environment, supporting its members and creating so many new opportunities. And we brainstormed about their priorities for next year. In the afternoon we listened to presentations of some of NCE’s members, it is incredible to see the amount of effort being done!   One key message of the day was about Namibia being in an employment crisis. And the enormous potential of tourism to help address this. We cannot agree more! Our Managing Director, Lara Potma, spoke about the opportunities tourism offers in terms of its value chain, infrastructure, guest experiences and marketing amongst others, which are incredible tools through which we can better integrate it with conservation. Let us all continue working together in building a tourism industry that actively betters our places and communities.  #wearetosco #conservation #sustainabletourism #namibia #powerpointfail
